clinicalPearls: ALECT2 is caused by deposition of leukocyte chemotactic factor 2, a protein of largely wild-type sequence, rather than by a classic amyloidogenic mutation.
It is a common cause of renal amyloidosis in specific populations, notably people of Mexican or Hispanic, Punjabi, First Nations, Native American and Egyptian ancestry.
The kidney is the dominant target, typically producing slowly progressive chronic kidney disease with only sub-nephrotic proteinuria, which is lighter than in AL or AA amyloidosis.
The liver is the second most commonly affected organ, and incidental hepatic ALECT2 is sometimes found at biopsy or resection.
Amyloid characteristically deposits in the renal cortical interstitium and glomeruli.
A homozygous common polymorphism in the LECT2 gene is associated, but the disease is not inherited in a classic Mendelian pattern.
There is no specific antifibril therapy, so management is supportive with attention to chronic kidney disease and its complications.
Accurate typing by mass spectrometry is essential, as ALECT2 is easily misclassified.
reference.pathophysiology: Leukocyte chemotactic factor 2 is a hepatically synthesised protein involved in inflammation and tissue repair. In ALECT2 the essentially wild-type protein deposits as amyloid, with a strong ancestral predisposition suggesting genetic susceptibility linked to a common LECT2 polymorphism rather than a destabilising point mutation. Fibrils accumulate preferentially in the renal interstitium and glomeruli, and in the liver, producing indolent organ dysfunction. Because proteinuria is characteristically modest despite significant renal impairment, the disease can be clinically silent until chronic kidney disease is advanced. The mechanisms triggering deposition of the normal-sequence protein remain incompletely defined.
additionalDifferentials: Other hereditary amyloidoses such as fibrinogen and apolipoprotein A-I types
Other causes of chronic kidney disease with modest proteinuria
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with Congo red staining showing interstitial and glomerular amyloid
Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry, which is essential to identify LECT2
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
Serum amyloid A and C-reactive protein to exclude AA amyloidosis
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging
SAP scintigraphy to assess organ burden
redFlags: Progressive chronic kidney disease with disproportionately mild proteinuria in a patient of at-risk ancestry
Unexplained hepatic amyloid found on biopsy
Declining renal function without an obvious alternative cause
reference.prognosis: ALECT2 is generally indolent, but renal involvement tends to progress slowly to end-stage kidney disease over years. There is no proven disease-specific therapy, so outcomes depend on chronic kidney disease management and on renal replacement or transplantation.
pitfalls: Misclassifying as AL or AA amyloidosis without mass spectrometry typing
Discounting amyloid because proteinuria is only sub-nephrotic
Overlooking the diagnosis outside the classically affected ethnic groups
Giving inappropriate chemotherapy on the assumption of AL amyloidosis

Confirm the amyloid type by mass spectrometry and exclude AL and AA amyloidosis before any misdirected treatment
General renoprotective measures and cardiovascular risk-factor modification
Monitoring of renal function, proteinuria and hepatic involvement over time
Renal replacement therapy by dialysis and consideration of kidney transplantation for end-stage disease
